operational-boundaries.title: Operational boundaries
operational-boundaries.description: What Connex can reach in your deployment, how support works, and how to report a problem usefully.

text: Connex is frequently run by the customer rather than by Connex. That changes how support has to work: there is no remote session for an engineer to join, and no diagnostic channel that phones home. Everything support needs has to come out of your own environment and be handed over deliberately.
This page explains what that means in practice, and how to give support enough to actually help.

items.title: A self-hosted deployment is yours
items.description: Connex has no remote access to it and nothing in the product reports usage or content back to Connex. The keys are generated in your environment and stay there.

items.title: The service processes your data to provide the service
items.description: Connex is not end-to-end encrypted. To score relationships, run searches and render reports, the application works with your CRM content in the clear. What differs between deployment shapes is who operates that application, not whether it can read the data.

items.title: Administrative surfaces are closed by default
items.description: The general-purpose management endpoints are switched off entirely. The health check is deliberately minimal, and the metrics endpoint requires a token before it will answer anyone.

items.title: The audit log is append-only
items.description: Audit entries are chained with an integrity secret and protected at the database level so the application cannot rewrite history.

items.title: Diagnostic state moves by bundle, not by access
items.description: When a ticket needs more than a reference code, an organisation administrator downloads a redacted bundle and hands it over deliberately. It carries readiness, configuration and an audit slice, never secrets, hosts, record values or people's names, and it collects no log content at all.

blocks.title: Quote the reference from the error screen
blocks.body: When a page fails, the error screen shows a short reference code. That code is the fastest way for whoever runs your deployment to find the exact matching entry in their own logs. Copy it exactly, and include what you were doing and roughly when.

items.title: Capture the reference
items.description: Copy the reference code from the error screen if there is one. If the failure was a save or an action rather than a whole page, note the exact time instead.

items.title: Say what you expected
items.description: The record you were on, what you clicked, and what you expected to happen. Whether it happens every time matters a great deal.

items.title: Hand it to whoever operates your deployment
items.description: On a self-hosted deployment that is your own team, and they can match your reference against their logs directly. On a Connex-operated deployment it goes to Connex support.

items.question: Can Connex support look at my data to debug something?
items.answer: Not on a self-hosted deployment, where Connex has no access at all. Anything support sees there is something your own team has chosen to send them.

items.question: Does Connex send usage data back?
items.answer: No. There is no telemetry channel back to Connex from a deployment Connex does not operate.

items.question: Who can see the audit log?
items.answer: Members of your workspace who hold the audit permission, and organisation administrators for organisation-level events. It is readable and exportable, but never editable.

items.title: Audit logs
items.description: What gets recorded, and how to read and export it.

items.title: Privacy and data requests
items.description: Handling disclosure, correction and deletion requests.

diagnostics-and-support.title: Diagnostics & support
diagnostics-and-support.description: Check your workspace's health yourself, and give support what it needs.

text: When something looks wrong, Connex gives you a page that answers the first round of questions without anyone needing access to a database or a server. It reports what your instance is configured for, which providers are ready, whether background jobs are running, and whether email is working.
You will find it under Settings, and administrators get an organisation-wide version covering every workspace.

items.title: Deployment and capabilities
items.description: Which edition this instance runs as, and for each capability whether the edition forbids it or it is simply not configured. Those are different problems with different fixes.

items.title: Provider readiness
items.description: AI, business-card reading, email, delivery channels and capture streams, each reported as ready or not.

items.title: Scheduled jobs
items.description: The latest run of each background job, with its most recent success and its most recent failure kept separately, so a run of failures never hides the last time it worked.

items.title: Email and secret storage
items.description: Whether mail is configured and usable, plus key-health counts for stored credentials. Only counts and status, never any stored value.

blocks.title: Opening the page contacts nothing
blocks.body: Everything on it is read back from saved configuration, so looking is always safe: it never calls your AI provider, your mail server or any connected account. Sending a test email is the only action on the page that reaches the outside world.

items.title: Confirm it is you
items.description: The test asks for a passkey first, like other administrative actions.

items.title: Check your own inbox
items.description: It only ever sends to your own address, and your address has to be verified. Nobody can use it to send mail to anyone else.

items.title: Read the result
items.description: You get the sending identity and the transport outcome. On a workspace that supplies its own mail server you also get an advisory note on whether SPF and DMARC records exist for that domain.

blocks.title: Three tests in five minutes, and the fourth says Failed
blocks.body: The test is limited to three sends every five minutes for each person in each workspace. Going over that limit does not produce a special message: the result comes back as Failed, looking exactly like a broken mail server, with a rate-limited reason code. If you have been testing repeatedly and suddenly everything fails, wait five minutes before believing it.

blocks.title: When you do need to raise a ticket

items.title: Quote the codes, not the screenshots
items.description: Findings on the page carry short stable codes, and a failure gives you a reference identifier. Those two things let whoever runs your deployment find the exact matching record in their own logs.

items.title: Say what you expected
items.description: The record you were on, what you clicked, what you expected, and whether it happens every time. That last one narrows the search more than anything else.

items.title: Know who your operator is
items.description: On a self-hosted deployment your own team holds the logs and can match your reference directly. Otherwise it goes to Connex support.

blocks.text: Handing diagnostics to support

If the page and a reference code are not enough, an organisation administrator can download a support bundle: a single redacted archive of your deployment's diagnostic state that you hand over deliberately. It is assembled on request, so it reflects the moment you asked.

blocks.title: What is and is not in it

items.title: Readiness and configuration
items.description: The same health picture the diagnostics page shows, plus allowlisted configuration and migration history.

items.title: An audit slice
items.description: Recent audit rows for the window you asked for, identified by account id only. No display names appear anywhere.

items.title: No secrets and no record values
items.description: No credentials, no hostnames, no CRM field values and no personal names. What was left out on purpose is listed in the bundle, so a missing file reads as a decision rather than a gap.

items.title: No logs at all
items.description: The bundle collects no log or journal content. Server logs cannot be narrowed to one workspace, so collecting them was deliberately left out rather than shipped unsafe.

blocks.title: Ask for a narrower window, not a bigger bundle
blocks.body: Assembly stops rather than trimming: there is a size ceiling and a time budget, and exceeding either is refused outright with a message asking you to shorten the period or narrow it to one record. If a bundle is refused, make the request smaller rather than trying again unchanged.

items.description: What Connex can reach in your deployment, and how support works without that access.

items.description: What the SPF and DMARC hints mean, and what still has to be done on your DNS.

deliverability-basics.title: Email deliverability basics
deliverability-basics.description: Why Connex mail does or does not reach an inbox, and what to check first.

text: Connex hands your email to a mail server and nothing more. It does not sign your mail, publishes none of the records that receiving servers look at, and cannot make a message land in an inbox on its own. It can now tell you whether two of those records exist, but only as a hint, and only for a workspace that supplies its own mail server. Whether your mail arrives is decided by the mail server you point Connex at and by the DNS records on your sending domain.
That is worth knowing before you debug a delivery problem, because the fix is almost never inside Connex.

blocks.title: The three records that decide your fate

items.title: SPF says who may send for your domain
items.description: A record on your domain listing the servers allowed to send as you. If the server Connex hands mail to is not covered by it, receivers will treat your mail as suspect.

items.title: DKIM signs your mail
items.description: Your mail server adds a cryptographic signature, and publishes the matching key in DNS under a selector name it gives you. Connex never signs anything itself, so this is entirely your mail provider's job.

items.title: DMARC tells receivers what to do
items.description: A policy record saying how to treat mail that fails the other two, and where to send reports. Start by only monitoring, read the reports, and tighten once you are confident.

blocks.title: The from address and the bounce address are the same here
blocks.body: Connex does not set a separate envelope sender, so the address your recipients see is also the address used for the checks. That keeps things simple, but it means the domain in your from address is the one that has to be properly set up. Ask your mail provider whether they rewrite it on the way out, because that changes which domain has to align.

blocks.title: Checking a workspace's own mail settings

items.title: Open the email settings for your workspace
items.description: This is where a workspace supplies its own mail server instead of the instance default. If your instance manages mail centrally, the setting is not available and there is nothing for you to do here.

items.title: Send yourself a test
items.description: The test uses exactly the settings you saved, with no fallback, and reports the transport result. It only ever sends to your own address.

items.title: Read what it proves
items.description: A successful test means the host, port and credentials work and the server accepted the message. It does not tell you where the message landed. This test checks no DNS records at all; the diagnostics test described below is the one that does.

blocks.title: Common symptoms
rows: No mail at all, and no error anywhere
Mail is probably not enabled on the instance, or the flow you expected has its own separate switch that is still off.
Mail arrives, but from an address you did not expect
Your workspace settings could not be used and the instance default was used instead. Your operator's log records this.
Almost always the DNS records on your sending domain, or a mail server that is not signing. Start with a DMARC report.
A test email works but real mail does not
The transport is fine. Look at the per-flow switches and at whether the recipient is suppressed or unsubscribed.

blocks.title: Bounces are only handled for campaigns
blocks.body: Bounce and complaint handling, suppression lists and unsubscribes exist for marketing campaigns, and only when your administrator has connected an email provider that reports receipts. Invitations, notifications, reports and password mail have none of that: they are sent, and if they fail, the failure is only visible in your operator's logs.
